mcqs.question: A dependency is overloaded and returning errors for 30% of requests. Every client retries immediately on error. What typically happens next?
options: The retries have no measurable effect on the dependency's load
The error rate improves, since retries give the dependency more chances to succeed
The added retry traffic increases load on the already-overloaded dependency, pushing the error rate higher — a retry storm
The dependency automatically load-balances the retries away from itself
mcqs.explanation: Naive immediate retries add to the exact load that's causing the errors in the first place, creating a feedback loop where more errors trigger more retries which cause more errors — a retry storm. Retries don't magically get routed away from the overloaded dependency or improve its error rate.

mcqs.question: Why does adding jitter to exponential backoff matter, given that clients already wait increasing amounts of time between retries?
options: Without jitter, clients that failed together stay synchronized and retry again at the same instant, still producing a spike
Jitter reduces the total number of retries a client will attempt
Jitter is only useful for read requests, never for writes
Backoff alone already fully prevents any synchronized retry spikes
mcqs.explanation: Exponential backoff alone still lets clients that failed at the same time follow identical schedules, so they retry in lockstep, just later — still a spike, only delayed. Jitter randomizes the wait to spread that spike out; it doesn't inherently reduce retry count or apply only to reads.

mcqs.question: A gateway promises clients a 2-second response time. Service A (called by the gateway) calls Service B with a 3-second timeout. What's wrong with this setup?
options: Nothing — each service should set its own timeout independently of its callers
3 seconds is always too short for any downstream call
Timeouts should never be shorter than 3 seconds regardless of the caller's budget
Service A's timeout to B exceeds the gateway's own budget, so A can end up waiting past the deadline it owes the gateway
mcqs.explanation: Per-hop timeouts must fit inside the caller's own budget, not be set independently — here Service A can wait up to 3 seconds on B alone, already blowing past the gateway's 2-second promise before A even responds. There's no universal minimum timeout value; it depends entirely on the budget being allocated.

mcqs.question: A client's "charge this card" request times out with no response. Is it safe to automatically retry it?
options: Yes, a timeout always means the server never processed the request
Yes, as long as the retry uses exponential backoff
It's only unsafe if the retry happens within 1 second of the original request
No — the server may have already processed the charge; retrying a non-idempotent write like this risks double-charging the customer
mcqs.explanation: A timeout only means the client didn't get a response in time — the server-side charge may have already succeeded. Retrying a non-idempotent write blindly can execute it twice; backoff timing and how soon the retry happens don't change that risk. The safe fix is an idempotency key or avoiding auto-retry on that write.
